correctness.rationale: Sequential stability is equivalent to choosing a maximal student at each remaining-set stage. For fixed permutation, stage independence and exchangeability give product a_m/m, hence product a_m for expectation. If an earlier stage has two maximal choices, both extend, so uniqueness requires a single maximal choice at every stage, with conditional probability product b_m. In t independent permutations, maximal students are t-dimensional Pareto maxima: integrate (1-prod v_r)^(m-1) to obtain Phi_t(m); a unique maximal exists iff all top-ranked student labels agree, with b_m=m^(1-t). Uniform-integrable product-of-uniforms integral yields the log asymptotic for fixed t. Independently checked all 6^6=46656 priority profiles at n=3,t=2 via direct blocking pairs; resulting distribution for Z=1..6 was (7776,14256,11664,9072,2592,1296), mean 11/4, uniqueness 1/6.

evidence: Kitahara–Okumura establish equivalence of weak M-stability and intersection-priority matching, but focus on mechanisms and efficiency, not a random number-of-stable-matchings product law. Bentley–Kung–Schkolnick–Thompson already count maxima of random coordinate sets; this local a_m factor is credited, not claimed novel. Pittel randomizes both sides rather than imposing perfectly common student rankings. No inspected source states the multiplicity/uniqueness factorization for this null model.

final_claim: For n students and n schools with common student school ranking and independent t uniform school priority orders, expected number of intersection-stable matchings equals product over m<=n of Phi_t(m)=sum_j(-1)^(j-1) binom(m,j)/j^(t-1); uniqueness probability is (n!)^(1-t); fixed t asymptotic log expectation is (t-1)n log log n-n log((t-1)!)+o(n). A general independent exchangeable restriction-consistent partial-priority factorization holds.
